#5050. COLDCARD bug goes undetected for 5 years despite 15 security reviews: Details

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Read the best crypto stories of the day in less than 5 minutes. Join to get it daily in your inbox.

Coinkite, the company behind Bitcoin [BTC] hardware wallet COLDCARD, has revealed that a security vulnerability remained undetected for more than five years, despite at least 15 independent security reviews, including AI-assisted research.

According to the 23rd November, 2026 postmortem published by Coinkite, the issue affected certain COLDCARD firmware versions released between 29th March, 2021, and 30th July, 2026.

Although the devices continued to generate valid recovery phrases and appeared to function normally, an underlying firmware error meant that the randomness used to create private keys was weaker than intended.

That said, the issue stemmed from a software integration error that caused certain Coldcard devices to use a weaker pseudo-random number generator instead of the intended hardware-based system.

This generator produced less unpredictable recovery phrases, making it easier for attackers to guess the private keys and access users’ Bitcoin. Although the recovery phrases appeared normal and passed some security tests, they did not offer the expected level of protection.

As a result, the vulnerability reportedly resulted in the theft of at least 1,789 BTC, worth approximately $114.7 million at the time. As of 18th November, Coinkite had received around 300 loss-related support tickets linked to 242 customer accounts. However, the actual number of victims could be higher.

That said, vulnerability significantly reduced the difficulty of reconstructing affected wallet seeds. According to Coinkite, the affected seeds had approximately 40 bits of effective entropy on Mk2 and Mk3 devices and 72 bits on Mk4, Mk5, and Q devices.

This was considerably weaker than the originally intended 128-bit security. This allowed attackers to use offline brute-force searches to reconstruct private keys and gain access to Bitcoin holdings without physically accessing the hardware wallets.

However, Coinkite did address the issue on 31st July and introduced additional security measures in August. Yet, it is still investigating the incident alongside law enforcement authorities and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security.

Up until now, the company has not finalized a compensation plan. Regardless, it has been advised that the affected users must generate entirely new recovery phrases and transfer their Bitcoin to new wallets.

This is because simply updating the firmware will not secure previously compromised recovery phrases.

All of this coincided with Ethereum researcher Justin Drake warning that artificial intelligence could potentially discover mathematical shortcuts to break the cryptographic systems protecting crypto private keys.

At the same time, crypto security losses surged 55% to $1.18 billion in Q3 2026, up from $763.97 million in Q2, while reported breaches increased from 67 to 107.

In that, compromised suppliers, delayed patches, and unaudited components accounted for 77% of losses, highlighting risks beyond smart contract vulnerabilities. Lastly, smart contract flaws also caused $569.5 million in losses, while access control and operational failures contributed to another $477.6 million.

#5049. VanEck is dropping Gemini from nearly $1 billion in Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana ETFs

Coinbase will remain the funds' custodian as VanEck ends its custody, clearing and staking arrangements with Gemini.

VanEck is ending its relationship with Gemini across three spot crypto ETFs, leaving Coinbase Custody as its remaining named custodian.

The asset manager disclosed in Nov. 19 regulatory filings that it had notified Gemini of plans to terminate its custody and clearing agreements for its Bitcoin ETF (HODL), Ethereum ETF (ETHV) and Solana ETF (VSOL).

The agreements are scheduled to expire in February 2027, and Gemini will continue to provide services until the termination takes effect. The decision also ends a separate arrangement under which Gemini facilitates Solana staking for VSOL.

The filings did not disclose the reasons for the termination or how much cryptocurrency VanEck currently holds with Gemini.

The three funds have attracted approximately $1.15 billion in cumulative net inflows since their respective launches and collectively managed $934.2 million in net assets as of Nov. 24, according to SoSoValue data.

VanEck's Bitcoin ETF accounted for the bulk of that exposure, with $977.1 million in cumulative net inflows and $848.2 million in net assets. Its Ethereum and Solana funds recorded cumulative net inflows of $151.6 million and $19.2 million, respectively.

VanEck's decision extends beyond asset safekeeping. Gemini also provides clearing infrastructure that helps the funds settle cryptocurrency transactions associated with ETF share creations and redemptions.

Under the existing arrangements, VanEck's funds can use Gemini Clearing to complete trades negotiated with liquidity providers that are also Gemini customers.

The service has supported cash-based orders, which require the funds to purchase or sell cryptocurrencies, and in-kind transactions involving the direct transfer of digital assets.

The scheduled February 2027 exit affects two services across VanEck’s HODL, ETHV and VSOL.

Coinbase Custody stays with all three funds. The filings name no successor to Gemini’s trade clearing service.

The lines track service appointments. The filings give no amount or timing for any transfers between custodians.

The connections trace each service described in the three November 19 termination filings across its scheduled effective date.

The lines track service appointments. The filings give no amount or timing for any transfers between custodians.

Coinbase will continue serving the Bitcoin and Ethereum funds under their existing prime broker agreements, while the Solana fund also maintains a separate custody agreement with the company.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

VanEck did not identify a successor to Gemini's clearing services or provide a timetable for any cryptocurrency transfers between the custodians.

VanEck's decision contrasts with arrangements at other major US crypto ETF issuers that have established relationships with multiple digital asset custodians.

BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust ETF (IBIT) uses Coinbase Custody as its custodian and has appointed Anchorage Digital Bank as an additional provider. Its latest quarterly report said the fund had no immediate plans to transfer Bitcoin to Anchorage.

BlackRock also maintains flexibility in its trading arrangements. The fund can execute Bitcoin transactions directly with third-party counterparties or through Coinbase Prime when processing cash-based creation and redemption orders.

Meanwhile, the Fidelity Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund maintains its primary custody and trade execution relationship with Fidelity Digital Assets, an affiliate of its sponsor. Fidelity has also appointed BitGo Bank & Trust as an additional custodian, although it reported no immediate plans to transfer Bitcoin to the company.

These arrangements allow BlackRock and Fidelity to retain additional custody providers without necessarily distributing their existing Bitcoin holdings across them.

VanEck's termination of Gemini's agreements moves in the opposite direction across three separate crypto investment products, increasing the importance of its remaining relationship with Coinbase.

Its September quarterly reports describe transactions conducted directly with liquidity providers, while earlier prospectuses also allowed alternative execution arrangements for certain trades if settlement failed.

Those existing arrangements could accommodate transactions previously handled through Gemini Clearing without VanEck appointing another dedicated clearing provider.

With the termination scheduled for February, VanEck's subsequent regulatory disclosures could reveal whether it intends to consolidate more of its trading infrastructure with Coinbase or establish new arrangements with other institutional service providers.

#5045. Fidelity Crypto Adds AAVE, LINK, UNI, Expanding Asset List to Eight

Home » Blitz news » Fidelity Crypto Adds AAVE, LINK, UNI, Expanding Asset List to Eight

Fidelity Investments adds three DeFi tokens to its retail lineup.

Fidelity Investments has added AAVE, Chainlink (LINK) and Uniswap (UNI) to its Fidelity Crypto trading service, expanding its supported digital asset list from five to eight. The addition lifts the number of supported assets from five to eight and brings three DeFi tokens to eligible US customers.

Fidelity announced the update on its official website and in an X post. The platform now supports Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), Solana (SOL), Litecoin (LTC), AAVE, LINK, UNI and the Fidelity Digital Dollar (FIDD), a US dollar-pegged stablecoin the company announced in January 2026.

Each new token is tied to a different part of DeFi. AAVE is the token for Aave, a lending protocol that mediates cryptocurrency lending and borrowing.

UNI is the governance token for Uniswap, a decentralized exchange. LINK is used in Chainlink, an oracle network that delivers external information such as price data to smart contracts.

Trading and custody are handled by Fidelity Digital Assets, a subsidiary licensed as a U.S. National Trust Bank. The service is available to eligible U.S. customers aged 18 and over residing in states where Fidelity provides the service.

Fidelity launched Fidelity Crypto for individual investors in 2022, initially offering Bitcoin and Ether. The latest addition follows Charles Schwab’s November 9 listing of Solana, Avalanche and Chainlink on its spot crypto platform.

Fidelity’s addition of AAVE, UNI and LINK extends a major US brokerage’s retail crypto offering to DeFi infrastructure tokens. It also adds to competition among traditional brokerages for crypto-active customers, following Schwab’s recent expansion.

#5044. French Senate Rejects Disclosure Rule for Crypto

French senators on Nov. 24 rejected a proposal that would have required taxpayers to disclose self-hosted cryptocurrency holdings exceeding €100,000.

They would have had to report those assets as of Dec. 31.

This would have been the case even if they had held the same coins since January without making any sales.

Two matching amendments to the French 2027 budget were rejected by the Senate during the first reading of the draft.

Senators Pascal Savoldelli and Anne-Sophie Romagny reintroduced the proposal after it briefly passed in the National Assembly earlier in the month.

French taxpayers must disclose their crypto assets held on foreign crypto platforms.

These amendments would have expanded disclosure requirements to wallets that owners directly control. This pertains to a wallet that is not managed by an exchange or another custodian.

The French National Assembly approved the €100,000 disclosure threshold in a 150-44 vote on Nov. 3. There were also eight abstentions.

The next day, the National Assembly voted down the entire revenue portion of the budget.

This vote brought down the wallet disclosure provision along with the rest of the budget.

However, the subsequent effort to revive the provision in the Senate was defeated.

It should be noted that the 2027 budget is still being considered at the time of writing.

The Senate also rejected two other crypto-related measures debated as part of the budget.

One was a provision to tax gains realized when holders exchange cryptocurrencies for certain stablecoins.

The second was a proposal to expand France's exit tax to include unrealized gains on cryptocurrencies held by taxpayers who move their tax residence outside the country.

#5043. Bitcoin’s crash protection could make its next selloff worse as US inflation data looms

Options dealers could amplify price swings between $58,000 and $64,000, even after much of Bitcoin's vulnerable futures leverage has been cleared.

A Bitcoin put can cushion losses for its buyer, while the trades a dealer makes to hedge the same option can make a fresh selloff harder to stop.

In its Nov. 24 report, Glassnode estimated that options dealers could reinforce declines by selling and rallies by buying when Bitcoin traded between $58,000 and $64,000. The US inflation report due Nov. 25 gives that setup a near-term test.

On a seven-day average, 1.7 Bitcoin puts traded for every call, the highest ratio since June 2022, according to Glassnode’s Nov. 24 report.

The put-to-call ratio for outstanding contracts separately reached its highest since May 2021. Put trading includes sellers and positions that serve purposes beyond crash protection, so the volume ratio shows where activity shifted without revealing who took which side.

A put gives its buyer the right to sell at a fixed price, or receive the equivalent cash payoff. The lower Bitcoin finishes below that price, the larger the payoff before the option's cost.

A dealer who sells the put takes the other side of that exposure and can hedge by selling Bitcoin or futures. As Bitcoin falls, the put becomes more sensitive to the decline, and the dealer may need to sell more to keep the hedge balanced.

Gamma measures how quickly an option’s price sensitivity changes. If prices reverse, a dealer in short gamma can buy back part of the hedge, adding to the rebound.

The feedback can be stronger when few buyers or sellers stand ready to take the other side, a pattern that researchers studying equity options found in less liquid stocks.

Glassnode estimated positive dealer gamma in the adjoining $56,000-$58,000 and $64,000-$66,000 bands. Dealers hedging positive gamma can buy weakness and sell strength, helping absorb a move. Those were modeled zones for one snapshot, and new trades or expiries can shift them.

A separate estimate from GEX Monitor from Nov. 24 also showed negative net gamma near $60,000, with the largest concentration by absolute exposure at that strike.

Glassnode’s Nov. 24 estimate put short gamma between $58,000 and $64,000. Bitcoin was near $59,700 later that day.

Within the estimated short-gamma band, dealer hedges can reinforce both a selloff and a rally.

The bands describe an estimate at one point in time. Dealer positions, liquidity and the influence of hedging can change as prices move, trades arrive or contracts expire.

Range widths are proportional to the reported dollar spans. Glassnode’s estimates use Nov. 24 data at 16:00 UTC. The later CryptoSlate observation at 21:12 UTC is rounded to $59,700. The paths illustrate short-gamma dealers hedging a move.

The bands describe an estimate at one point in time. Dealer positions, liquidity and the influence of hedging can change as prices move, trades arrive or contracts expire.

Glassnode estimated that nearly 90% of the leveraged futures longs it had flagged between the prior week’s Bitcoin price and its realized price had cleared. Realized price is the average price at which coins last moved.

The selloff had already pushed into a $55,000-$62,000 cluster of positions at risk of liquidation.

Futures liquidations occur when traders can no longer meet their margin requirements, so options dealers rebalance as prices move even if nobody faces a margin call.

Glassnode reported $4.3 billion of net outflows from US spot Bitcoin ETFs over the 20 trading days covered in the report.

The Bureau of Economic Analysis scheduled its October inflation report and revised third-quarter GDP for Nov. 25 at 8:30 a.m. ET. The inflation report includes the personal consumption expenditures price index (PCE).

Trading Economics listed a 0.3% monthly consensus for core PCE, which excludes food and energy. The Cleveland Fed’s model estimated 0.27% separately.

Investors are watching what the data means for rates after the Fed’s October minutes showed broad support for more tightening if the economy evolved as officials expected.

At derivatives exchange Deribit, Wednesday’s daily Bitcoin options are scheduled to expire at 3 a.m. ET, five and a half hours before the release.

They had about 6,172 BTC of open interest, around 1.4% of outstanding coin-settled Bitcoin options on Deribit, in Deribit’s Nov. 24 options data, against 111,797 BTC in the Nov. 27 monthly expiry.

Deribit’s Nov. 24 coin-settled Bitcoin options book showed 6,172 BTC of gross open interest in the daily expiry before PCE and 111,797 BTC in the monthly expiry after it. The exchange publishes open interest with an eight-hour lag.

Source: Deribit options data · Deribit expiry policy · Deribit public API changelog · BEA release schedule

CryptoSlate estimated the effect of removing Wednesday’s expiry using coin-settled contracts expiring within 30 days.

Assuming dealers held the long side of every call and the short side of every put, contracts set to outlast the release accounted for about 93% of the Nov. 24 model’s net negative gamma.

The Nov. 27 expiry alone accounted for about 49% of the original total, leaving about 7% in Wednesday’s expiry under the same assumptions.

The calculation holds prices and positions at their Nov. 24 readings, so actual gamma can shift as Bitcoin moves and expiry approaches, and the public exchange data counts contracts without identifying dealer positions.

The Nov. 27 put open interest was spread across several strikes, including $60,000, $63,000 and $64,000. At the same $60,000 strike, annualized implied volatility was 50.4% for Wednesday’s expiry, 56.1% for Thursday’s and 54.6% for Friday’s.

The higher Thursday and Friday marks cover the inflation release and other risks over longer periods.

A hot print could lift rate expectations and start a selloff that short-gamma dealers reinforce with hedge sales.

A cool print could ease rate pressure and prompt a rebound that the same dealers reinforce by buying. If inflation comes in close to forecasts, the GDP figures and demand for Bitcoin could matter more.

For the rest of the week, watch whether Friday’s expiry changes positioning and whether spot buyers return. The NYSE closes for Thanksgiving, ending Friday’s core equity session at 1 p.m. ET.

If dealers turn long gamma or liquidity improves enough to absorb their trades, the same catalyst could produce a smaller swing.

The Wednesday outflow was not the first large one this month. On Nov. 17, about 312 billion SHIB were withdrawn from exchanges, according to CryptoQuant. On the same day, the number of SHIB holders on Ethereum passed 1.7 million, according to Etherscan.

CoinGlass data also shows that since late 2024, the total SHIB balance on exchanges has gone down by 19.18 trillion tokens, or 20.54%, to 74.19 trillion, and over the same period, the price of SHIB fell by 88.39%. Most of the 24-hour outflow came from exchanges that CoinGlass groups as "Others," as their combined SHIB balance fell by 88.5% to 70.93 billion tokens. Over the same period, the SHIB balances of Binance and OKX barely changed, and Coinbase, Bitfinex and Bitstamp added SHIB.

As a result, in the week when the price of SHIB fell to levels last seen in 2021, exchanges lost more SHIB in a single day than over the previous six days combined, according to CoinGlass data.

#5040. Australian Crypto Investors Turn to Loans Ahead of 2027 Tax Reform

Home » Crypto Market News » Australian Crypto Investors Turn to Loans Ahead of 2027 Tax Reform

Upcoming capital gains tax reforms are prompting crypto holders to reconsider how they access cash without selling their digital assets

One in five Australian cryptocurrency investors would consider borrowing against their digital assets rather than selling them, as upcoming tax changes push holders to rethink their financial strategies.

A survey commissioned by digital asset wealth platform Nexo found that 22.7% of Australian crypto holders would consider borrowing against their holdings instead of selling, compared with 10% of other investors.

The findings come as Australia prepares to overhaul its capital gains tax (CGT) system from July 1, 2027.

Nexo surveyed 1,000 Australian investors this October to examine how major expenses and rising living costs affect investment decisions.

The results suggest that crypto holders are more inclined to avoid selling their investments when they need additional funds.

Beyond the 22.7% considering borrowing, another 19.7% said they had delayed or decided against selling their crypto holdings.

Crypto investors can borrow against their existing holdings instead of selling them for cash. This allows them to access money while keeping their Bitcoin or other digital assets, and potentially benefit if their value increases.

The trend comes against a broader backdrop of financial pressure. According to the survey, 29.4% of all investors had delayed, reduced or cancelled a major purchase or financial plan over the previous 12 months.

The upcoming CGT reform is another factor investors may need to consider.

Under Australia’s current system, eligible individuals, trusts and partnerships can receive a 50% capital gains tax discount on assets held for more than 12 months.

From July 1, 2027, this discount will be replaced by cost base indexation and a 30% minimum tax on eligible gains.

Under transitional arrangements, gains accrued before that date will remain eligible for the existing 50% discount, while gains accumulated afterward will be subject to the new rules.

Crypto ownership in Australia is at a record high, with 2.79 million Australians holding or trading cryptocurrency, according to the figures cited in an Australian investor Study.

That equals about 24% of the country’s 11.5 million investors, up from roughly 15% in 2023, making crypto as widely held as exchange-traded funds (ETFs).

As ownership expands, the demand for financial products that allow investors to access liquidity without selling their holdings could also increase.

Consequently, as their holdings rise in value, more investors may look for ways to cover major expenses without selling their crypto.

The new CGT rules could make some investors think twice before selling crypto that has increased in value. As a result, more holders may consider borrowing against their holdings to cover major expenses without having to sell their assets and potentially trigger a capital gains tax bill.

Solo Bitcoin Miner Scores Again, Hitting $191,000 Jackpot Against the Odds

A lone Bitcoin miner has once again defied steep odds, single-handedly mining a block and pocketing a reward worth roughly $191,000, a windfall that normally flows to the industrial-scale operations dominating the network.

Blockchain data shows the miner solved block 977057 on Nov. 22, earning 3.12871270 BTC, made up of the 3.125 BTC base subsidy plus about 0.0037 BTC in transaction fees.

The block was found through Solo CKPool, a service that lets independent miners point their machines at the network and keep the entire reward if they get lucky, rather than pooling hash power and sharing payouts.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Solo miners command a tiny sliver of Bitcoin’s total computing power, and finding a block means being the first to guess a winning number against the combined might of massive mining farms running warehouses full of specialized machines.

The odds for a small setup are often likened to winning a lottery, which is why each solo success tends to draw attention.

And yet, it’s far from an isolated event, and solo Bitcoin miners have hit jackpots like this with increasing regularity throughout 2026. Scores worth around $300,000, $225,000, $210,000 and $200,000, as the price of Bitcoin fluctuates, have all landed with individual miners over the past year, some using only modest or rented hardware.

The frequency underscores that while the probability for any single miner is minuscule, the sheer number of people trying means someone occasionally beats the house.

The timing is notable against the backdrop of a strained mining industry. Bitcoin miners have been selling their holdings and pivoting infrastructure toward the AI boom, squeezed by thin margins, a lower post-halving subsidy and a Bitcoin price that has slumped well off its highs.

For large operators, those pressures have made mining a tougher business; for the solo miner who just won, it’s a rare, outsized payday.

What a solo miner does with the reward is up to them, and the win doesn’t change the economics for everyone else still grinding away. But these occasional long-shot victories remain a point of fascination in Bitcoin, a reminder that the network’s lottery, however improbable, still pays out to the little guy now and then.

At current prices, with Bitcoin trading around $62,000, the 3.13 BTC reward works out to roughly $191,000, though the dollar value shifts with the market.

The DeFi protocol faces mounting pressure as its largest borrowers owe $115 million and depositors struggle to access their funds.

Sky, the $3.4 billion lending protocol, is facing mounting pressure across its DeFi ecosystem as a withdrawal crisis coincides with a multibillion-dollar contraction in its stablecoin supply.

The liquidity shortage centers on Sky's stUSDS product, which uses stablecoin deposits to finance loans backed by staked SKY.

DeFi analyst Ignas pointed out that the lending product operates separately from the collateral backing DAI and USDS, as well as the strategies generating returns for ordinary sUSDS savings holders.

However, the sharp decline in SKY's price has intensified concerns over loans taken out by some of the ecosystem's largest participants, particularly Sky co-founder Rune Christensen.

A Nov. 19 investigation by blockchain analytics firm Bitquery found that Christensen's associated positions were backed by 3.58 billion SKY, representing approximately 15% of the token's circulating supply.

Bitquery identified 25 borrowing transactions without a repayment on the current lending engine between May 2025 and Nov. 19, during which the positions accumulated approximately 10.4 million USDS in unpaid interest.

Three of the four identified positions also fell below their required collateralization thresholds, according to Bitquery's analysis, while automatic liquidations were disabled.

The four vaults owed 74.46 million USDS as of Nov. 24, while Sky Frontier Foundation owed another 40.17 million USDS. Their combined borrowing represents approximately 72% of the stUSDS vault's assets.

The scale of Christensen's SKY exposure complicates his repayment efforts, as selling substantial quantities on the open market could weaken the token's price and the collateral backing other loans.

On Nov. 23, Christensen said he was exploring a direct sale of some of his SKY holdings to institutional investors. Crypto entrepreneur Du Jun subsequently expressed interest in acquiring his entire position.

Unlike Christensen, Sky Frontier Foundation already holds stablecoin savings that could substantially reduce its borrowing.

On-chain data reviewed by CryptoSlate showed that the foundation held approximately 27.9 million USDS in redeemable savings on Nov. 24.

Deploying those funds would allow the foundation to repay roughly 69% of its outstanding debt without selling SKY, releasing liquidity equivalent to nearly 18% of the stUSDS vault's assets.

The repayment could also substantially reduce the foundation's financing expenses.

A Nov. 23 governance forum post highlighted that the foundation was paying nearly 50% in annualized borrowing costs while earning approximately 3.8% on its savings.

At those rates, repaying 27.9 million USDS would reduce the foundation's net annualized financing costs by approximately $12.8 million.

The foundation previously disclosed that it borrowed against its locked SKY holdings to finance operations, leaving it to determine how much of its savings it can commit to repayment.

However, the speed at which depositors previously drained liquidity shows how short-lived any relief could be under the vault's existing withdrawal mechanism.

On Nov. 23, Christensen's wallet repaid 3 million USDS. Within 24 seconds, ten withdrawals totaling approximately the same amount followed, with the first two alone accounting for roughly 83% of the repayment.

Sky Frontier Foundation could cover much of its loan from savings. The prior repayment shows how fast cash can be withdrawn.

The foundation’s savings could cover about 69% of the loan. The stUSDS vault pays withdrawals as transactions clear against a shared balance.

The repayment shown for the foundation is conditional on its deciding to deploy its savings. The observed withdrawals were paid from the shared pool and do not identify ultimate recipients or guarantee access after a future repayment.

The rapid depletion has prompted calls for a proportional withdrawal queue that would distribute returning liquidity according to depositors' holdings.

A separate governance proposal would deploy $40 million to $50 million from Sky's reserves to acquire SKY directly from borrowers and apply the proceeds toward their outstanding loans.

Neither proposal has received formal approval, while the foundation has yet to commit its savings toward repayment.

#5032. Bitcoin ‘As Important as It’s Ever Been’ if Inflation Rises, Coinbase CEO Says

"Bitcoin investors tend to sell BTC when there's a big IPO. Then they come back."

That's Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong's take on Bitcoin investor behavior, less than a week after the record-breaking $93.5 billion IPO of Claude creator Anthropic.

"Historically, people rotate out of it to take advantage of a big IPO. Then they come back in," Armstrong wrote on X earlier today.

The limited window of opportunity to invest in an IPO helps explain the behavior Armstrong described. For an investor to buy at the IPO price, there's only a certain period during which they can request an allocation of shares. After that, the price is determined by the market.

On Nov. 19, Anthropic went public on the Nasdaq, and that brief window of opportunity mattered.

Shares were priced at $83, up from the $70-$78 range indicated just two days earlier. Anthropic's stock, trading under the ticker ANT, opened at $111.50.

If you bought at that opening price, you paid about 34% more per share than an investor who received an allocation at the IPO price.

When the IPO closed on Nov. 20, 1.127 billion shares had been sold, including 147 million additional shares purchased by underwriters exercising their option.

Of the $93.5 billion in gross proceeds, Anthropic itself received around $91.6 billion. The rest went to existing shareholders.

There was also a separate $26 billion private placement involving investors such as Microsoft, Nvidia, Google and others. In total, the combined transactions were valued at $119.5 billion.

As for the longer-term case for holding BTC, Armstrong's point concerns investors' expectations about the future purchasing power of their money.

"If you think there is going to be more inflation and money printing in the future, bitcoin is as important as ever."

At the heart of the matter is Bitcoin's 21 million supply limit.

If you expect governments to continue expanding the money supply, you may still be excited by the prospect of a major IPO. And you may sell some of your BTC to participate in it.

Armstrong's argument is that the window of opportunity to participate in a major IPO eventually closes.

However, the reasons investors bought Bitcoin in the first place may remain long after the newly listed stock starts trading.

#5028. Why Nvidia Needed Jensen Huang Back—And What His Return Really Changes

Why Nvidia Needed Jensen Huang Back—And What His Return Really Changes

Jensen Huang did not unveil a breakthrough chip on Monday. He simply got his old job back—and Nvidia shares surged more than 30%, while the Nasdaq jumped nearly 7% in midday trading.

The reaction revealed something more consequential than Wall Street’s fondness for a charismatic CEO: investors had spent 11 days confronting how much of the AI boom runs through one person.

Huang, who resigned November 12 amid revelations about extramarital affairs and an unproven Chinese espionage allegation involving a former customer executive, has returned as CEO, president, and director.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Nvidia with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Nvidia’s board says his reinstatement poses no national security risk, based partly on input from senior U.S. officials. Its independent investigation, however, is not over.

The company did not stop making chips. CFO Colette Kress became interim CEO, Harvey Jones took over as Nvidia’s first board chairman, and executives insisted the technology roadmap and customer commitments remained intact.

Kress presided over earnings that showed roughly $116 billion in quarterly sales and projected about $130 billion for the following quarter—staggering numbers that still failed to calm the market.

Inside Nvidia, the transition looked considerably less routine. During the first companywide meeting without Huang, staff had submitted about 700 questions, many concerning compensation and board transparency.

Kress promised pay increases and extra stock awards in December, months earlier than planned. Executives took turns assuring workers that the company could serve customers without Huang; some employees nevertheless discussed leaving if his absence became permanent.

The pushback extended outside headquarters. An online petition gathered roughly 200,000 names, though signers’ claimed employee or shareholder affiliations were not independently verified. Altimeter Capital’s Brad Gerstner and Atreides Management’s Gavin Baker, whose firms had disclosed about $2.1 billion in Nvidia shares, urged a deliberate succession process that kept Huang’s return possible. It was an unusual message to directors searching for a replacement: don't rush to replace the founder.

This letter was sent to Nvidia's board today.

Absolutely share @altcap belief that this letter outlines minimum acceptable standards. pic.twitter.com/ST2f5TMAa1

— Gavin Baker (@GavinSBaker) November 14, 2026

In other words, Nvidia couldn’t survive the scandal—not the one about Huang cheating, but the one about Huang leaving.

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and turned graphics processors into the hardware behind modern AI. But his power also lies in the relationships surrounding those chips: cloud giants buying entire data centers of GPUs, developers locked into Nvidia’s CUDA software, suppliers building its next systems and policymakers deciding which markets it can serve.

Reuters reports that he has overseen roughly 60 direct reports and personally shaped major deals and product decisions.

He has also become a financier and ambassador for the AI ecosystem. Nvidia has invested in companies including CoreWeave and Nebius, which buy computing hardware to rent AI capacity to others.

That web of investment, sales, and financing is precisely why his disappearance unnerved markets far beyond Nvidia. After his outsting, Chinese customers delayed or canceled orders while leadership was unsettled; the whole Nasdaq index and the wider S&P500 crashed and odds for a bubble pop spiked to more than 70% on prediction markets.

Then, on Monday, minutes after his return, CoreWeave and Nebius shares each jumped more than 20% alongside Nvidia which had its best day in history—Huang also probably had his best day ever, too.

To have a grasp of Huang’s influence, one just needs to follow the money.

Elon Musk backed the reinstatement campaign; Y Combinator chief Garry Tan and Epic Games’ Tim Sweeney were among other prominent supporters. Bill Ackman celebrated Monday with “sanity prevails.” Trump pressed the case personally, later saying his intervention was “very important” and that the administration assured directors there was no national security obstacle to Huang’s return.

That backing helps explain the whiplash: On November 17, Jones said the board would not reinstate Huang, citing conduct inconsistent with Nvidia’s standards. Six days later, the same directors voted unanimously to bring him back. They say meetings satisfied them about his candor and leadership, but have not explained exactly what changed. Supporters see recognition of an indispensable founder; critics see a board yielding to powerful outsiders.

Bullish analysts argue that restoring Huang reduces execution and talent-retention risk. Dan Ives has framed Nvidia as a $300 stock with Huang versus $225 without him, while Melius Research upgraded the shares to “buy” with a $220 target.

Yet Monday’s roughly 30%-plus rebound followed a Friday close of $125.53; even near $165, Nvidia remains well below its October peak. Buying the comeback means paying much more for the same projected chip sales.

The other side is harder to price. Michael Burry criticized the reversal, and legal scrutiny of Huang, Nvidia’s export controls and its board continues. The company is establishing a board committee for national security and export-control oversight and recruiting a chief compliance officer.

None of that resolves the fundamental AI question: whether customers can earn enough on massive infrastructure spending to sustain Nvidia’s growth.

Huang’s return repairs a missing link between Nvidia, its customers, Wall Street, and Washington. The 11-day crisis showed how much confidence that link carries—and how vulnerable the AI trade becomes when it breaks.

What he has not yet won back is an unquestioned mandate to lead.

#5027. Bitcoin’s selloff deepens as Trump tariffs and hot inflation revive market fears

Options traders are rushing into puts at the fastest pace in four years while realized investor losses reach levels last seen during the FTX collapse.

Bitcoin fell to $57,470 on Wednesday as hotter-than-expected US core inflation and the announcement of new tariffs intensified selling across risk assets.

The Nasdaq 100 extended its losses to 2.9%, reversing the optimism that followed Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO earlier this week.

Data released by the US Bureau of Economic Analysis on Nov. 25 showed that the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index, the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge, rose 3.8% annually in October, its second-highest reading since April 2023.

Core PCE inflation, which excludes food and energy prices, accelerated to a three-year high of 3.3%, beating economists' 3.2% forecast.

Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, said the stronger-than-expected core reading showed that price pressures were spreading across the economy beyond the recent energy shock.

The report follows increases in both consumer and producer price inflation, with financial markets now assigning a greater than 97% probability to a quarter-point interest rate hike on Dec. 9.

That would mark the Fed's second rate increase of 2026, lifting its benchmark rate to between 4% and 4.25%. Twelve months ago, investors were anticipating three rate cuts this year.

Meanwhile, President Donald Trump's administration announced a new round of proposed tariffs targeting 14 major US trading partners following an eight-month investigation into foreign industrial policies.

The measures include additional tariffs of 20% on Chinese imports, up to 35% on Vietnamese goods, and up to 25% on imports from India, Taiwan and South Korea. The European Union faces duties of up to 20%.

The announcement opens another front of uncertainty for investors already grappling with the prospect of higher borrowing costs.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

André Dragosch, Bitwise's European head of research, expects this market turbulence to persist, saying:

“Market volatility will likely stay elevated in the short term until uncertainty around inflation and the outlook for monetary policy fully resolve.”

The deteriorating macroeconomic backdrop comes as Bitcoin investors show signs of financial distress comparable to the depths of the 2022 bear market.

Blockchain analytics firm Glassnode reported that Bitcoin's correlation with the Nasdaq 100 has climbed to its highest level since September 2022. Over the past 60 trading days, Bitcoin has consistently underperformed the index on both up and down days.

That weakness has coincided with a surge in demand for downside protection across Bitcoin's options market.

According to Glassnode, the seven-day average put-to-call trading volume ratio reached 1.7 last week, its highest level since June 2022. The corresponding ratio for outstanding options contracts climbed to its highest level since May 2021.

“The last rush into puts like this was June 2022. Bitcoin was near $20,000 in the middle of the capitulation. The final low came five months later, below $17,000.”

The growing pessimism extends beyond derivatives markets. CryptoQuant CEO Ki Young Ju said Bitcoin investors are underwater at historical capitulation levels, while Glassnode reported that realized losses, relative to recent capital inflows, had reached their highest level since FTX collapsed in November 2022.

Institutional demand has also weakened, with US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds registering $4.9 billion in net outflows this month.

Glassnode identified Bitcoin's realized price of $53,200 as the next major threshold should the cryptocurrency close decisively below its June closing low of $58,500.

Every previous major Bitcoin bear market saw prices fall below the realized price before bottoming out. Reaching that level would require a further 7.4% decline from Wednesday's reported low, as investors confront the prospect of tighter monetary policy and a prolonged withdrawal of institutional capital.

#5021. North Korea Moves $247 Million of Binance Hack Loot Through Bitcoin Mixers

North Korea Moves $247 Million of Binance Hack Loot Through Bitcoin Mixers

North Korea’s hackers have now funneled at least $247 million from the record $6.4 billion Binance theft through Bitcoin “coinjoins,” a mixing technique designed to sever the trail between stolen funds and their origin, blockchain analytics firm Elliptic said.

The figure, roughly a month after the Oct. 29 hack, reflects just the funds pushed into coinjoins, which pool many users’ Bitcoin into a single transaction so the coins can’t be traced.

Notably, almost all of it was coordinated by a single known individual: the operator of Kruw, the most widely used coinjoin coordinator for Wasabi Wallet users. That operator “refuses to block funds such as these,” Elliptic co-founder Tom Robinson told Decrypt in an email, which is why the firm expects the laundering to continue.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Bitcoin with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

The mixing accelerated sharply in mid-November. On Nov. 17, the attacker emptied five of the nine largest Ethereum addresses tied to the theft, shifting about 488,000 ETH ($860 million) into fresh batches.

Those are being steadily swapped into Bitcoin through the Thorchain bridge and then sent into coinjoins, often within hours, the same playbook North Korea used after the $1.5 billion Bybit hack in early 2025.

The operation has spanned more than 27,000 wallets across at least 16 blockchains, roughly 55 services and some 90,000 transactions. Elliptic stressed it is clearly automated but found no evidence AI agents are directing it, pointing instead to conventional software, with fixed timing, set amounts and pauses that resemble human working patterns in Pyongyang.

Elliptic earlier found the hackers even minted their own worthless meme coins to shuffle funds through liquidity pools, one of several obfuscation tactics stacked together alongside cross-chain bridges, asset swaps and lending-vault hops.

The FBI has attributed the theft to the North Korean group TraderTraitor, and Binance has said it will cover all customer losses.

Still, little has actually been cashed out. About $2.85 billion has been frozen, and roughly $2.35 billion remains parked in theft-linked addresses, including the 18,270 BTC taken directly from Binance, which hasn’t moved since the night of the hack.

Elliptic expects the funds to be converted to Bitcoin, mixed and eventually cashed out through over-the-counter brokers over a period of months, the point at which they can still be intercepted.

With the Kruw operator declining to block the flows, though, the mixing shows little sign of slowing.

#5019. AI agents are reshaping the job market and less-experienced workers are feeling it first

New research raises questions about how workers will acquire professional experience as companies increasingly automate junior-level tasks.

US job advertisements for less-experienced workers grew more slowly at listed companies with greater estimated exposure to AI agents.

A Nov. 23 research paper examining 34.8 million US job advertisements across 1,784 publicly listed companies found a widening gap in recruitment demand between experienced and less-experienced professionals after the release of Anthropic's Claude Code 2.0 in September 2025.

The researchers found that a one-standard-deviation increase in estimated exposure to AI agents was associated with 4.54% lower job posting growth for non-senior positions over the six months following the release.

The disparity became more pronounced when the researchers examined recruitment based on experience requirements. Positions requiring up to five years of professional experience recorded 4.87% lower posting growth associated with the same increase in AI exposure.

The study compared how estimated AI agent exposure related to ad growth by seniority and experience at sampled US listed firms.

Higher estimated exposure was linked to slower posting growth in non-senior titles and in ads asking for up to five years of experience.

The results concern posting growth at sampled listed firms. Exposure is estimated from stock returns and aggregate OpenRouter activity. The senior-title and six-plus-years estimates were statistically inconclusive. The analysis leaves causal effects and actual hires unresolved.

Table 7, Panel B, in the Nov. 23, 2026, arXiv revision. Coefficients of −4.539 and −4.868 are shown to two decimal places on a common linear scale, using the authors' approximation of percentage growth. The baseline and comparison track average monthly postings.

The results concern posting growth at sampled listed firms. Exposure is estimated from stock returns and aggregate OpenRouter activity. The senior-title and six-plus-years estimates were statistically inconclusive. The analysis leaves causal effects and actual hires unresolved.

Meanwhile, the researchers found no statistically significant relationship between AI exposure and posting growth for senior positions or roles requiring at least six years of experience.

Please enable JavaScript to verify and send this form.

The difference between the two groups was statistically significant, suggesting that emerging AI capabilities are affecting recruitment priorities unevenly across experience levels.

Economists Nicola Borri, Anton Cheremukhin, Yukun Liu and Aleh Tsyvinski used Anthropic's Sept. 29, 2025, Claude Code upgrade as a dividing point in their analysis. The upgrade expanded Claude's ability to work autonomously, letting it take on more complex coding tasks with less human intervention.

To estimate corporate exposure to these emerging capabilities, the researchers examined how closely companies' stock returns tracked growth in AI agent usage on OpenRouter, a platform providing access to multiple AI models.

Companies with higher exposure scores were subsequently more likely to discuss AI agents in regulatory filings and earnings calls.

The researchers found no statistically significant relationship between estimated AI exposure and job posting growth before the Claude Code upgrade. The divergence emerged in recruitment data covering October 2025 through March 2026.

The findings raise longer-term questions about how companies will develop their future workforce as AI agents become capable of performing tasks traditionally assigned to less-experienced employees.

Junior positions have historically provided workers with opportunities to develop the technical expertise, institutional knowledge, and professional judgment required for senior roles.

If companies increasingly automate that work while still demanding experienced professionals, workers entering the labor market could face fewer opportunities to gain the qualifications employers continue to seek.

That could eventually create a recruitment problem for companies themselves as they compete for experienced workers while narrowing the career pathways that produce them.

WH associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT, is also a fan of the fit and vast color palette. “They never ride up or move around, which is hard to find in a running short,” she says. With tons of colors and sizes to choose from, you can't go wrong.

New Balance is a top brand in the running world, and the RC Short is one of my faves. It runs slightly big, but I love the extra breathing room during a sweat session.

The lightweight, flowy construction uses the brand’s quick-drying tech fabric (a polyester and spandex blend) to wick moisture from the skin. The breathable design promotes tons of airflow, creating a cooling effect while I run—especially ideal during scorching hot summer runs.

The seamless, interior lining reduces chafing and irritation, while the waistband features an adjustable drawstring to customize the fit. It’s also not too tight—some liners can feel like you’re wearing a diaper (hate). As for storage, there’s a back pocket for securing small running essentials and even tiny snacks like a granola bar when you’re on the move.

A pair of high cut shorts, such as the Alo Match Point Short, is a running staple. The high-cut at the thighs keeps things perfectly airy and flowy for optimal coolness when I get overheated, more so than the Lululemon Hotty Hot Short.

This construction, paired with its moisture-wicking polyester fabric, creates the perfect breathable running shorts. While it’s a bit short at just over two inches, there’s still great coverage with a built-in brief, and I find it doesn’t show too much skin.

WH style contributor Lily Wolhner also appreciates this loose style for various workouts. “My favorite part about this short is that it’s never clingy, so it doesn’t ride up the thigh or need constant re-adjusting while you’re working out,” Wolhner says. “I’ve worn it for months and recently tested it during a 45-minute strength and HIIT workout, as well as an hour-long cross-training workout—I never felt over-exposed or uncomfortable in it.”

By the looks of the elastic waistband, I expected it to dig into my skin—wrong. It felt comfortable, although it’s important to note this short does run big, so I suggest sizing down.

We love a two-for-one, and this short from Brooks is ideal for both trail running and running at the gym. It has light compression with a built-in tight liner that doesn’t sacrifice mobility.

The mega-durable polyester fabric resists tears and moisture, which makes it ideal for trail running in tough terrain. “I love the high waist, the zipper pocket to carry my keys, and the tight shorts under a looser short aesthetic,” Katz says.

Two waistband pockets are impressively large and can even fit a water flask, so you can always stay hydrated during your jogs.

I personally don’t love compression-lined shorts because I like to feel totally free, but if you prefer extra coverage and double layers, this short is ideal.

If you want a no-frills pair of shorts at an affordable price point that will stand the test of time, the Under Armour Play Up 3.0 belongs in your running gear collection. I’ve owned multiple pairs for years in eye-catching colors, and they’re still in good condition with no pills—even after dozens of runs and wash cycles.

The lightweight knit fabric made from smooth polyester has an anti-pill finish for extra durability, and is impressively comfy. Plus, it hides embarrassing sweat stains post-run, despite the slightly thicker material.

The waistband uses a wide elastic band that provides a secure fit without any adjustable features. However, I find it still fits roomy and allows for a full range of motion.

It includes deep side pockets but no enclosure, so I don’t recommend stashing anything super important besides fuel, like energy gels. I wear it the most for shorter, mid-distance runs and whenever I want to add a pop of color—it has 21 color options!

I usually don’t gravitate toward compression shorts since I don’t like feeling constricted, but the Athleta Salutation Stash 5-Inch Short offers the perfect amount of tightness. It hugs my thighs with gentle compression, while the high-rise waistband distributes pressure evenly for a secure fit without digging in. Plus, the two deep side pockets offer convenient storage for longer runs.

The smooth, double-knit fabric is buttery-soft and offers great coverage. While on the thicker side, it conceals sweat stains well—a huge win during long-haul runs. I wouldn’t say it feels the most breathable compared to other shorts in this guide, but the nylon and lycra blend wicks away sweat and dries fast.

Another huge selling point? The fabric’s UPF 50 protection, which prevents UV radiation from scorching your thighs. This is my favorite feature as someone fair-skinned and prone to nasty sunburns (IYKYK). Aside from its fabric, I love that it has a matching jacket for a coordinated workout set.

Tracksmith’s Van Cortlandt Shorts combine retro styling with a performance-driven design that makes them a winner both on and off the track. It’s made from a lightweight mesh fabric to maximize airflow, paired with an antimicrobial finish to help combat odor by wicking away sweat and limiting bacteria buildup during intense runs.

After summer runs when I’m dripping with sweat, I noticed zero smell—and that the short dries at the speed of light.

Like our best overall, it’s quite short at 2.5 inches, so if you prefer a longer style, you should look to other styles in this guide. On the flip side, it doesn’t disrupt my range of motion during speed work or long runs. As for fit, I found it runs true to size, but make sure to consult the size chart as always.

Running shorts with sweat-wicking fabric are the way to go, Katz says. Most shorts use a blend of polyester, spandex, and/or nylon, which lifts moisture from the skin while staying flexible during movement. Based on testing, it’s best to avoid cotton since it doesn’t dry nearly as fast and clings to the skin when wet.

It’s important to determine what kind of rise and inseam you desire. High-waisted running shorts offer more coverage and tummy control, while a mid-rise waist sits right at the hips. Ultimately, what you find most flattering for your body type is the best option.

The inseam is the length from the crotch to the bottom. A longer length will show less skin but may disrupt the range of motion, while some running shorts favorites, like the Lululemon Hotty Hot High-Rise Lined Short, offer a 2.5-inch option if you like a mini fit.

As for an interior liner or compression, this will make running shorts fit more snugly. “Compression is a matter of preference, but the goal in this material is to boost recovery,” says Katz. If you want a less constrictive fit, it’s probably best to avoid that feature.

In addition to my own testing, Women’s Health associate health and fitness editor Addison Aloian, NASM-CPT also extensively tested tons of running shorts to determine whether or not they’re the real deal. Each pair was worn during training runs or races for anywhere from three weeks to even three years to see how they performed and held up.

Essential features considered were materials, inseam, pockets, durability, and adjustability. Additionally, I asked a running coach for their go-to running shorts and guidance on how they should fit.

#5014. France’s Senate Rejects Rule Forcing Bitcoin Holders to Declare Self-Custody Wallets

France’s Senate has rejected a proposal that would have forced bitcoin holders to report self-custody wallets worth €100,000 or more to the tax authorities, along with two other crypto tax measures in the 2027 budget.

Senators voted down two identical amendments on Nov. 24 during debate on the first part of the 2027 finance bill. Both would have required taxpayers to declare crypto wallets they hold directly, outside a crypto service provider, when the total value inside reached at least €100,000 on Dec. 31 of the tax year.

The first, amendment I-2447, came from Sens. Pascal Savoldelli and Pierre Barros and the Communist-led CRCE-K group. The second, amendment I-2992, came from Sen. Anne-Sophie Romagny and seven other senators. The government opposed both, and both were rejected.

Backers argued that France already makes taxpayers declare accounts on foreign crypto platforms, just like foreign bank accounts. Wallets that holders manage themselves, without an intermediary, escape any such obligation.

“They have become the digital equivalent of the undeclared safe,” the CRCE-K group wrote in its amendment, adding that tax authorities can’t see them, check gains on them or reach them in an estate or when a holder moves abroad.

Romagny’s version pointed to a gap in the numbers. Crypto holders in France realized €3.5 billion in gains in 2021, but only €400 million in digital assets were declared to the tax administration that same year, the amendment said. It proposed fines of up to €10,000 for failing to declare.

The National Assembly had approved the same wallet rule on Nov. 3. It fell away the next day, when deputies rejected the entire revenue section of the budget. Senators then took up the same measure as an amendment to the budget.

Senators also rejected two other proposals from the CRCE-K group. Amendment I-2421 would have ended France’s tax deferral on swaps into electronic money tokens under the EU’s MiCA rules. That would have made converting bitcoin into a regulated stablecoin a taxable event.

Amendment I-2428 would have pulled crypto into France’s exit tax on unrealized gains for people who move their tax home abroad. It counted all crypto toward the €800,000 threshold, including coins held in self-custody or outside France.

David Amiel, France’s minister for public action and accounts, argued against the wallet rule, saying the EU’s DAC8 directive already puts reporting duties on crypto firms. He said he was “more circumspect” about a “purely declarative” obligation that would not help authorities track crypto used in money laundering or tax fraud.

The Senate’s finance committee also opposed the measures, and rapporteur general Christine Lavarde recommended rejecting all three. Lavarde noted that the wallet amendments drew on a recommendation from a Senate information report filed in June, and she left the question of the threshold to the government.

Holders have also raised safety concerns. In August, bitcoiners were warned of wrench attacks after France’s tax authority confirmed a data breach affecting hundreds of thousands of people.

Reporting rules for platforms are still expanding. The National Assembly is set to debate approval of the OECD’s Crypto-Asset Reporting Framework, or CARF, which shares crypto tax data between countries, on Dec. 7.

The wallet fight is not fully over. The Senate is still working through the 2027 budget and is set to vote on the full bill on Dec. 9, before a joint committee of both chambers takes it up.

#5013. Visa is testing an AI economy where agents work and humans collect the paycheck

The payments giant is testing a system that allows verified AI agents to complete paid assignments and generate stablecoin income for their owners.

Visa is testing how AI agents can use traditional banking credentials to qualify for paid work that settles in stablecoins.

On Nov. 22, Visa Crypto Labs head Cuy Sheffield announced an update to the company's Visa CLI wallet that allows users to verify their AI agents and access paid assignments on Taskmarket, a marketplace for AI-generated work.

The initiative expands Visa's experiments in agentic commerce beyond enabling AI systems to spend money on behalf of their owners.

Under the new arrangement, agents can generate income by completing tasks, with payments made in Open USD, a dollar-denominated stablecoin, on the Tempo blockchain.

The service is currently available by invitation to eligible US users, who must register a personal Visa card and authenticate it using a one-time code from their issuing bank.

Once an owner authorizes an agent, Visa registers its public signing key in the company's Agent Directory, allowing participating platforms to verify its credentials.

Taskmarket uses that directory to authenticate agents when they claim assignments or submit completed work. New jobs posted through Visa require verified agents by default, although requesters can remove that restriction.

The arrangement gives Visa a role in determining which AI agents qualify for economic opportunities while blockchain infrastructure handles their earnings.

Taskmarket introduced settlements on Tempo on Oct. 22, expanding its marketplace beyond USDC-denominated assignments on Coinbase's Base network. Its Visa-linked worker verification feature is currently exclusive to Tempo.

Visa automatically screens assignments before agents can undertake them. Owners running agents on their own computers can authorize them to claim and submit screened tasks without individual approval, while remotely hosted agents require human authorization.

Payments are typically released when requesters accept completed assignments, with the proceeds transferred directly to the agent owner's Tempo wallet.

By using cardholder authentication to qualify agents for work that pays in stablecoins, Visa is testing a model in which its verification infrastructure can support economic activity that settles outside its traditional card network.

The invitation-only rollout will test whether those credentials can gain traction among businesses and individuals commissioning AI-generated work.

#5010. Why One Math Proof Has AI Experts Warning Humans Might Soon Lose Control

Why One Math Proof Has AI Experts Warning Humans Might Soon Lose Control

Meta Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang warned Sunday that artificial superintelligence is approaching—and that humanity may be unable to control systems far smarter than itself.

In an essay on X titled “Superintelligence is Arriving,” Wang said the next year could determine how people live alongside machines capable of improving themselves. His catalyst was an extraordinary mathematics result involving Anthropic’s Claude.

“Superintelligence is arriving. How humanity acts over the next year will have great consequence on what future world we live in,” Wang wrote.

You can now act on the news you read: Go long or short Anthropic with perpetual futures, all from your Decrypt Money Account.

Wang called the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis a greater intellectual achievement than building the atomic bomb, which he described as a “homework problem” by comparison. The breakthrough, he wrote, came with help from an “alien mind that we don’t understand.”

The warning carries extra weight because Wang runs Meta Superintelligence Labs. Mark Zuckerberg brought him aboard in 2025 after Meta invested $14.3 billion for a 49% stake in Wang’s startup, Scale AI.

On Friday, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge said he and Claude had proved the Riemann Hypothesis, a conjecture about prime numbers that had resisted mathematicians since 1859. The claim arrived a day after Anthropic’s massive IPO.

Alpöge released roughly 17 million lines of code in Lean, a system that checks mathematical proofs. On Saturday, the Lean and Mathlib communities certified that the code proves the correct statement; researchers are still working to explain its mathematics in conventional form.

For Wang, the result suggests raw reasoning power is no longer AI’s central limitation. He argued that the remaining hurdles involve specialist knowledge, experimentation, and the tools needed to apply intelligence in other fields.

That includes AI research itself. If machines can redesign more capable successors, Wang fears a cycle of recursive self-improvement could move faster than human monitoring or intervention.

“It is hard to imagine a world where humanity can maintain control over fully unconstrained recursive self-improvement,” he wrote. He also questioned human control over hypothetical systems “1000x smarter” than people.

Wang criticized the industry’s “lazy thinking” that superintelligence is inevitable and the only question is making it safe. “We should not be okay with a ‘handover’ of society to AI,” he wrote, advocating technology that strengthens human decision-making.

In a Monday follow-up, he said Meta had delayed its Muse launch for months over safety concerns and backed industry safeguards. Zuckerberg, he added, wants most computing power devoted to serving customers rather than unrestricted self-improvement.

Meta nevertheless has its own ambitions. Its Muse Wonder models, released in October, compete with systems from OpenAI and Anthropic, making Wang both a critic of the race’s direction and a leading participant.

Not everyone accepts his leap from mathematics to superintelligence. NYU professor Andrew Gordon Wilson argued that proving an existing conjecture is different from inventing new mathematical frameworks such as calculus or relativity.

“Nothing compares to proving the Riemann Hypothesis in terms of sheer intellectual might”. I disagree. The introduction of calculus, general relativity, and quantum mechanics, are more profound intellectual achievements. Creativity, taste, and intuition is the difference.

— Andrew Gordon Wilson (@andrewgwils) November 23, 2026

The Riemann result demonstrates a remarkable human-AI collaboration, but it does not prove that autonomous superintelligence exists.

Wang has urged the industry to change course while Meta continues developing the systems he fears could eventually exceed human oversight.

#5008. The 8 Best Standing Desks for Walking Pads, Tested and Reviewed

From budget picks to tricked-out options for a better WFH space.

Women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

You log a lot of time at your desk, making it fair to wonder how to create a workspace that’s as comfortable and healthy for you as possible. If sitting on your butt all day isn’t your idea of a good time, it makes sense to consider investing in a walking pad. To create a seamless workspace, you’ll need a special desk to go with that. The best standing desks for walking pads allow you to cruise along as you work, while still providing all the usual trappings you expect from a desk.

While TikTok is packed with happy-looking people working this way, the treadmill desk is more than a trend. Research ties sitting all day with a higher risk of developing back pain and even issues with cardiovascular health, making it a good idea to try to get up and move as much as possible during your day.

“Prolonged sitting has been linked to a number of health concerns, which is why many people are turning to standing desks,” says Andrew J. Bach, DO, a physiatrist at Cedars-Sinai Spine Center in Los Angeles “A standing desk allows you to get your usual computer-based work done while on your feet, and it comes with several benefits over sitting all day.” (He lists off better circulation, less strain on your back, more calories burned, and better digestion as just a few.)

But proper form is critical with these. “People should keep in mind how long they have been in a certain position, and their posture specifically,” says Meg Darmofal, DPT, a physical therapist at Michigan State University. You don’t want to shrug your shoulders, reach too far forward, bend over, or crane your neck up or down to see your screen, she says—all of those can put you at risk for developing aches and pains.

To find the best standing desks for walking pads, we consulted experts and had Women's Health editors test several popular models in their own workspaces. Our top pick is the Uplift Standing Desk V3, thanks to its easy height adjustments, customizable design, and compatibility with a walking pad. Ahead, find our favorite options for different budgets, spaces, and work-from-home setups.

While everyone has different needs in a standing desk, the Uplift V3 is packed with enough features and adjustability to make it a good fit for most. This motorized desk has a height range of 22.6 to 48.7 inches and comes in a wide range of tabletop widths and desktop styles, giving you plenty to choose from.

The desk has an impressive 355-pound lifting capacity, so you can pile a lot on it. WH copyeditor Deanna Martin tested the V3 alongside a walking pad and loved how easily the setup transformed her home office. The desk moves up and down with the touch of a keypad, making it easy to switch between sitting, standing, and walking throughout the workday.

Martin also liked the customizable accessories, which include storage options and even a hammock. There's also a companion app that tracks your standing progress and estimated calorie burn, though you'll need a Bluetooth adapter to connect it to the desk. Best of all, she found the entire setup super easy to assemble.

At over $600, the V3 is certainly an investment. But its versatile design, smooth height adjustments, and 15-year warranty are worth the price point.

It’s fair to expect to pay more for a motorized standing desk, but this Flexispot option manages to deliver that important feature with a relatively low price tag. The desk moves between 28 and 47.6 inches, giving you plenty to work with. It also has four height presets operated by an LED control panel, and a relatively roomy desktop space.

The desk includes a hook for your headphones or bag, allowing you to keep them in close reach while you work. It also can handle 176 pounds of weight, which should be plenty to work with. While it doesn’t have as many features as pricier desks like the Uplift 3, it’s still a solid, sturdy option to support you through your workday and comes much more affordably.

Whether you already have a desk you like or just don’t want to splash out for a totally new model, a standing desk converter can be a good middle ground. This option from Rocelco simply plops on top of your existing table to create a standing desk, so you can use a walking pad without replacing your entire WFH setup.

While some standing desk converters are small, this one can hold up to two large monitors, a laptop, and more. There’s a retractable keyboard tray, although it may not extend far enough for everyone's needs. The height adjustment is manual, but easy to do with the turn of a dial. There’s even a grommet hole to help you organize your cords, giving you a lot of the perks of a standing desk without the full commitment. Just make sure your existing desk and converter are tall enough to accommodate your walking pad.

A contoured standing desk allows you to get in close to your workspace, with an ergonomic design that can help you maintain a comfortable position while walking on a treadmill. This Fully Jarvis desk is sleek and comfortable, with a gently sloping and curved front that feels natural under your arms.

During testing, we were able to put this desk together quickly. It has a very sturdy feel, which is helpful when you’re walking while using it. The desk also thoughtfully includes an outlet and USB/lightning charger, so you can plug in your computer without having to bend over. The motor adjusts easily, although it can be a little choppy when you move up and down. Overall, we found that it was easy and comfortable to use. It looks and feels like a high-quality desk thanks to its bamboo surface and sturdy steel frame, making this a workspace you’ll use for years.

Having a little extra storage space can go a long way when you're trying to keep your home office organized. This Sanodesk standing desk features built-in drawers to stash away your office clutter. It's also motorized, so you can easily adjust the height when you want to sit, stand, or hop on your walking pad.

WH Designer Taryn Colbert tested the desk for two weeks and gave it a four out of five. She liked its spacious, easy-to-clean surface and preset heights. “It’s perfect,” she says, adding that it was “easy to put together for a person thats not very handy.”

Her biggest gripes? She wished the power plug were positioned farther toward the back of the desk, rather than toward the front and side, and would have preferred a long, slim drawer for additional storage.

This electric standing desk from Veken has a compact design that won't take over your home office, along with a motorized height adjustment system that makes it easy to switch between sitting and standing. There are also programmable height presets, so you don't have to find your preferred position every time.

WH Fitness Editor Cori Ritchey tested the desk for two to four weeks and gave it a five out of five. She was super impressed by how sturdy it felt, even when raised to its maximum height. “It feels well made for a desk that the buyer assembles (no shaky IKEA feeling here, even when at its max height!),” she says. Ritchey also liked the easy-to-use height adjustments and wide range of positions.

Her biggest gripe was the size. While the 36-inch desktop was great for occasional use, she wished she'd gone up a size for everyday work. She also found the textured surface a little tricky to clean after spills.

This walking pad features a removable desktop that attaches to the treadmill's railings, giving you a convenient spot for your laptop or tablet while you clock your steps. WH Lifestyle Director Lindsay Geller tested the setup for over a month and gave it a five out of five. She especially liked how sturdy the desktop felt once attached and how easy it was to remove. “This is a really great way to get a second desk without actually committing to buying a full desk,” she says, noting that she shares a home office with her husband. She also found assembly straightforward, putting the entire setup together by herself in about an hour.

The desk is admittedly basic, and the treadmill doesn't offer adjustable incline. Geller also found the walking surface a little narrow for jogging, making this a better option for walking while working than more intense workouts.

Every standing desk has either a set height or height range. Bach points out that height is a “key factor” in your desk. “If you’re especially tall or short, make sure the desk can adjust to a level that works for you,” he says. Just keep in mind that you’ll want to include the height of your walking pad when figuring out the right standing desk height for you, since you’ll be on top of it while you use your desk. “Returning a bulky standing desk can be a hassle, so it’s best to get the right fit from the start,” Bach says. Ideally, your desk should be high enough that you can type comfortably while standing on your walking pad, without having to hunch over or raise your shoulders.

Not all standing desks are adjustable, but many are—and it’s a nice feature to have. “Being able to easily lower and raise the desk is important because, in some scenarios, returning to sitting is good as well,” Darmofal says. Some desks can be heavy and awkward to move manually, which can be frustrating if you plan to switch between sitting and standing during the day, Bach says. “Motorized options are the most convenient, since they transition with the push of a button,” he adds. (Just keep in mind that motorized options tend to cost more.)

At the end of the day, this is still a desk, and you need one that will hold your stuff. Make sure you factor in space to hold your computer, pens, notepad, water bottle, and anything else you usually have on your desk. If you're using a walking pad, you'll also want enough room for your keyboard and monitor so you don't have to lean forward while walking.

It’s important to make sure that your desk’s legs and any footing are wide enough to leave space for your walking pad to slip between. Pay close attention to the walking pad dimensions and desk dimensions, leaving a little room around the pad so you’re not jamming it in there.

We should also note that a lot of our standing desk selections below don't come with a walking pad (though the Sharper Image Treadmill Desk is an all-in-one option), meaning it's an additional expense. If you don't already have one, make sure to check out our under-desk treadmill buying guide.

I consulted with Bach and Darmofal to help identify what to look for in standing desks for walking pads. From there, I researched top models, narrowing the field based on criteria like comfort, adjustability, and ease of use. Because everyone has a different experience, I also paid close attention to customer reviews and prioritized desks with overwhelmingly positive feedback.

From there, Women's Health editors put several standing desks to the test in their own workspaces.
